demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
The event happened because of the way I acted
I should have protected others and I failed

issues.item: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, contamination appraisals are clinically atypical and hard to reconcile unless there was a specific disgust/violation element to the death exposure. The other selected appraisals ('Bad Coper' and 'Self-Comparison') fit bereavement-related PTSD more plausibly, but 'Contamination' points toward a different trauma phenomenology (e.g., assault or abuse) and is not coherent with the provided trauma type/profile.

issues.item: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one,' these two appraisals imply substantial personal responsibility for causing or entering the traumatic situation. That is hard to reconcile with an unexpected death unless there are special circumstances not reflected anywhere else in the profile. A clinician would question whether these items fit this trauma type as stated.

vignette:
Nadia stepped down from the bench for the last time on a Friday afternoon, three weeks before her husband Samir died. She had presided over her final case—a custody dispute—with the same measured authority she had carried for thirty-two years. At seventy-five, she was still sharp, still feared by young attorneys who stammered through their arguments, still respected by the clerks who called her “Judge” even in the elevator. She had planned to retire quietly, to spend more time with Samir in the garden they had planted when their children left home. But Samir had collapsed in that garden on a Tuesday morning, reaching for a fallen fig, and by the time the parameders arrived, his heart had already stopped.

Nadia had been inside, reviewing a brief she no longer needed to review. She heard the thud through the kitchen window and thought it was a branch. When she found him, his face was pressed into the soil, his hand still open. She called 911, she performed chest compressions—she had learned CPR thirty years ago for a first-aid course and never used it—but she knew, even as she pumped his ribcage, that he was gone. The parameders told her she did everything right. She did not believe them. In the weeks that followed, she replayed that morning obsessively, not the moment of finding him, but the minutes before: the decision to stay inside, the brief she had no reason to read, the way she had waved him out to the garden alone. She had acted as though he would always come back.

What frightened Nadia most was not the memory of his body, but the certainty that she should have prevented it. She had been a judge for three decades; she had built a life on the conviction that careful action could shape outcomes. Now she was haunted by the opposite belief: that the event happened because of the way she acted—because she had not gone with him, because she had not insisted he wait for her to finish her coffee. She told herself that a reasonable person would have sensed something was wrong. She told herself that she should have protected him, and she had failed. The word “should” became a splinter she could not remove.

Her daughter Leila called every evening. Nadia answered only every third call, and only to say she was fine. She had stopped attending the mosque on Fridays because she could not bear the women who touched her arm and said, “At least he went quickly.” She had stopped going to the grocery store because she once saw a man with Samir’s posture—the same slope of the shoulders—and had to leave her cart in the aisle. She had stopped reading legal journals because every article about negligence or duty made her chest tighten. The retirement she had anticipated now felt like a prison sentence. She spent most days in the armchair by the window, watching the garden grow wild, certain that a good wife would have kept it alive.

Her avoidance had consequences she had not foreseen. Leila stopped calling every evening and began calling once a week, her voice thinner each time. Nadia’s youngest grandson, who had once loved to sit in her lap and pretend to hold court, now asked his mother why Grandma was mad at them. Nadia knew she was losing them, but the effort of pretending to be fine felt heavier than the isolation. She had come to believe that her reactions since the event—the sleeplessness, the irritability, the inability to concentrate—proved something she had always feared about herself: that she was a lousy coper, that her composure on the bench had been a costume, and the real Nadia was someone who could not hold herself together when it mattered.

What finally brought her to seek help was a letter. It came from the state bar association, thanking her for her service and inviting her to a reception for retired judges. She held the crisp paper in her hands and felt a wave of nausea so intense she had to sit down. The letter was not threatening—it was kind, even warm—but it demanded that she re-enter a world where she had once been competent, and she was certain she would be exposed. She called Leila that night, not to talk, but to ask for the name of a therapist. She was not hoping to feel better. She was hoping, at most, to stop feeling that she had failed the only person who had ever truly seen her.
